Morgan Commodities Research Despite the improving tone in domestic Chinese copper use, our projections suggest refined imports into China this year will be about 23% _lower_ than 2012 levels. Though this would still result in a net import volume of 2.4 million mt, our sense is a drop in these trade flows is not widely expected in the market. Moreover, to the extent that it is anticipated by some, we believe those observers expect falling imports to lead to falling copper prices. Indeed, as a general rule of thumb, it seems that conventional wisdom has come to believe that stronger Chinese copper use—and higher copper prices— _require_ rising Chinese copper imports. Thus, in coming months, reports of slacker refined copper imports into China may initially spur selling pressure in futures markets, even as the annual average LME cash copper price in 2013 increases over 2012, if we are correct. In this report we run through some of the dynamics behind the downshift we expect in trade volume and discuss implications for the global copper market over the next 12 months. According to Chinese national statistics and our estimates, Chinese refined copper imports reached a record high 3.4 million mt last year, translating to a monthly average of 283 kmt. Annual exports also achieved a record (270 kmt), bringing net refined imports to 3.1 million mt, just 0.4% above the previous high in 2009 ( **Exhibit 1** ). In 2009, Chinese refined copper imports were driven by a surge in metals use and stockbuilding, spurred by aggressive stimulus spending and a cyclically low price (LME 3-month troughed at $2,845 per mt on December 24, 2008). In 2012, the drivers for net imports were similar, even if less forceful. Our calculations show that Chinese refined copper use increased by 7% in 2012, compared to 8% growth in 2011, 25% in 2009, and compound growth of 11d% per year since 2004. Although the slowdown in China’s copper usage growth rates is real and likely durable, it is important to note that the 2011 demand base was already 53% larger than 2008. Last year’s 7% growth in domestic copper use required 540 kmt of additional cathode, alone amounting to 3% of global use. China’s demand _growth_ was larger than the entire copper use of Brazil in the same interval. ### **See page 5 for analyst certification and important disclosures.** **Commodities** **Colin P. In addition to meaningful physical demand growth in 2012, stockbuilding also contributed to China’s large net imports of refined metal last year. We note that the LME cash copper price averaged $7,958 per mt in 2012, a 10% discount from the prior year’s average $8,813 per mt. On a peak to trough basis, cash prices moved from a high of $8,737 per mt on February 9th to a low of $7,283 per mt on June 8th, providing a 17% lower transaction price for the buyer at the latter price as opposed to the former. In the prior year, when import flows began picking up, the drop from peak to trough was even larger: cash prices skidded by 34% from a year-high of $10,179 per mt on February 14th, 2011 to a year-low $6,721 per mt on October 20th, as the European recession began. This average savings of $855 per mt between 2011 and 2012 is significant and helps explain why Chinese merchants opted to acquire and build material at this value price, in anticipation of their future procurement requirements from international markets. Especially skilled procurement traders may have saved as much as several thousand dollars per mt relative to prior and future costs. We estimate refined copper inventories in Shanghai bonded warehouses not affiliated with exchanges increased by over 500 kmt in 2012 and now stand around 650 kmt, or the equivalent of 26 days of projected Chinese refined copper use in 2013. 

In building an accurate picture of China’s copper usage, it is important to look beyond refined import data to imports of copper in other forms, which also increased significantly in 2012. Between January and November of last year, copper concentrate imports increased by 18.3% yoy to a record 6.9 million mt. Scrap imports increased by 4% yoy for the same period, reaching 4.4 million mt on a gross basis—the highest level since 2008. Copper alloys and blister imports increased by 38.0% and 36.4%, respectively.  Overall, we calculate that China’s total copper imports in 2012 in copper content terms were 8.3 million mt. This quantity is far higher than was achieved in 2009 (6.9 million mt), when strong demand (responding to low price) and poor availability of scrap led to an astonishing 118% increase in refined copper imports while scrap imports collapsed as availability dried up. 

## **Outlook for Chinese copper imports** 

We project that Chinese refined copper imports will fall by about 23% yoy in 2013, as users draw from the stockpile accumulated in 2011 and 2012. In o

ur baseline scenario, we anticipate a decline from 3.4 million mt to 2.6 million mt—a 790 kmt decrease. We currently forecast Chinese refined copper demand growth of 7% in 2013, or 566 kmt of incremental tonnage. The latest data packages show improving Chinese demand driven by a moderate pick-up in the housing sector, normalization of end product stocks, and an overall faster pace of infrastructure development following increased NDRC approvals from summer 2012. Downstream, the demand picture is tight; stocks at semi-fabricators and smelters are reportedly covering around one week of consumption. Inventories of end-use products are also being drawn down. For example, inventories of air conditioners at major producers have reportedly fallen from over 10 million units in early 2012 to just over 7 million units in late 2012 (less than one month of production). For the near term, we believe current refined stock levels are ample enough to forestall any significant need for restocking, and thus we expect copper users to exhibit a preference to run with hand-tomouth inventories, sustaining the a trend of the past few years. **Exhibit 2: China's imported copper** Percent share of total imports by copper content 100%

Morgan Commodities Research We expect the increase in Chinese refined copper demand will be met through growth in domestic copper concentrate production (up 6% in 2013F) and an increase in copper feedstock imports. We project China will import just under 2 million mt of copper contained in concentrates this year and 2.7 million mt in copper contained in scrap and blister (12% YoY growth) ( **Exhibit 2** ). This supply will support 14% growth in Chinese refined copper production in 2013, driving total output to 6.5 million mt, in our view. We estimate that significant tonnage is still sitting in and around Shanghai: almost 1 million mt, including both bonded and exchange stocks. Two factors will likely reduce these inventories over the next 12 months: (1) an easing credit environment including 2 to 3 more RRR cuts and liquidity management (we note that Chinese CPI ticked up to 2.5% YoY in December), and (2) reduced appetite for preparing for expected Chinese copper use through cash and carry inventory management. Our forecast for refined copper use in China in 2013 is 8.9 million mt, 2 Colin P. Fenton (1-212) 834-5648 colin.p.fenton@jpmorgan.com **Global Commodities Research** Metals Weekly 16 January 2013 leading us to conclude that 2.6 million mt of refined imports (or 217 kmt per month) will be required to bridge the gap with domestic production and the flow of inventories through supply chains. We expect inventory channels to be relatively lean by year end, opening the windo

w for restocking heading into 2014. 

## **Implications for risk and valuation** 

An 800 kmt drop in China’s refined copper import appetite, all else equal, implies significantly better availability in cash markets outside of China, with some of that metal likely to show up in LME warehouses. This is likely to depress associated premia.  These emerging trends are already evident.  Refined copper imports into China in 4Q2012 dropped by 20% relative to the average for the first three quarters, exhibiting the normal seasonal trend of slacker imports toward year-end, despite the overall strength in imports in 2012. This pattern has occurred in four of the past six years, with an average decline of 20%. The only two years that have bucked the seasonal trend in the past six years were 2008 and 2011, when imports surged by 48% and 76%, respectively, against the average for the first three quarters of those years ( **Exhibit 3** ). Importantly, these counter-seasonal increases in imports occurred against the sharpest price declines of the past five years ( **Exhibit 4** ). 

The inventory increases we expect in LME warehouses will likely blunt upward momentum in bid prices for LME metal, especially in 2Q2013. However, we do not think the inventory gains will be large enough to prevent the 2013 average price from increasing on 2012, for four main reasons.  First, a gradual drawdown of Shanghai bonded warehouse stocks would remove an overhang of inventory from the Chinese copper market that has been a source of uncertainty for some time. We expect that the pick-up in Chinese copper demand will initially be met by further de-stocking, rather than from new imports. We anticipate that Chinese inventories will be brought down to a level which would require some amount of restocking by the end of 2013. So, there is a flow dimension to our view, with the annual average for imports likely masking considerable variability in the monthly trade numbers. Second, we expect that the copper market will look through weakness in lower Chinese refined imports toward the more encouraging 



outlook for physical demand. Third, we note that while refined imports are likely to weaken by about 23% YoY (if we are right), China’s total trade call on the global copper market (including refined, blister, scrap, and concentrate) is likely to decline by a less significant 4% on the back of stronger imports of copper feedstocks. This inter-product dimension is important and must not be overlooked. Our models show Chinese feedstock imports will increase by about 9% YoY in 2013. Finally, we note that while a lower import volume into China implies softer cash markets in various jurisdictions outside of China, the underlying global balance is tightening, albeit modestly.  Our forecast for 2013 continues to expect a global deficit of 38 kmt (–0.2% of global consumption).
